newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin says Russia has no territorial claims.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says Russia has no territorial claims.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, setting out priorities in border policy, said on Wednesday Russia had no territorial claims on other countries and ruled out any changes in its frontiers.
In a written declaration published by the presidential press service, Yeltsin sent a thinly veiled message to separatists in Chechnya that Moscow would not meet their demands for full independence.

"The Russian Federation has no territorial claims on other states and proceeds towards the completion of international and legal registration of its borders responsibly and without conflict," Yeltsin said.
"It denies any territorial claims on the Russian Federation from other states."

In remarks which appeared to apply to Chechnya, Yeltsin said the main threats to national interests included the "display of nationalism, ethnic and regional separatism, conflicts of a religious nature".
He did not specifically mention Chechnya or any other independence-minded Russian regions.

The 65-year-old president, who is in a sanatorium outside Moscow preparing for a heart operation, has repeatedly ruled out full independence for the southern region despite rebel leaders' continued demands to break away.
His latest comments were made in a policy document described by the presidential press service as the Foundations of the Russian Federation's border policy.

The document's implications, if any, were not clear for a dispute with Japan over four islands off northern Japan which were seized by Moscow in the closing days of World War Two or for the demarcation of Russia's long border with China.
Russia also has a dispute with Estonia over Moscow's refusal to recognise a 1920 peace treaty and border deal.
